To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the apparent compressibility is a function of the compressibility of the pure solvent and of the compressibility and the volume of the solute, and (b) the compressibility of a protein is not the same as that of a pure protein.
the classical approach for the calculation of the compressibility of solvents in highly dilute solution is too small because the correlated volume fluctuations in the solution are neglected.
the apparent compressibility is a function of the compressibility of the solute and the compressibility of water.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question whether the hydration effects can be explained by the correlated volume fluctuations.
the development of an improved theoretical framework for the interpretation of ultrasonic measurements of the compressibility of highly dilute solutions.
the question of how the compressibility of solute molecules is influenced by the solvent.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the compressibility of solute is a function of the compressibility of the solvent, the volume fluctuations of the solute, and the correlation between solute and solvent volume fluctuations.
the classical approach is not applicable to highly dilute solutions and that the compressibility is not a property of the solute but rather a property of the solution.
the apparent compressibility is not a property of the solute, but a property of the solution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the apparent compressibility is a function of the compressibility of the protein, the compressibility of pure water and the correlation between the volume fluctuations of the protein and the solvent.
the apparent compressibility is not a property of the solute but a property of the solution.
the apparent compressibility determined by ultrasonic methods can be used to determine the hydration properties of proteins, if the correlated protein-water volume changes are taken into account.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the compressibility of a protein solution is determined not only by the compressibility of the protein and water but also by the correlated fluctuations of protein and water.
it is necessary to consider correlated volume fluctuations in the analysis of compressibility and sound speed measurements.
the classical approach is not able to describe the compressibility of highly dilute solutions and that the hydration effects can be explained by correlated protein-water volume changes.
